screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build practical fluency with the operational side of AWS Direct Connect. You will learn the pricing components that drive cost decisions, how to use CloudWatch metrics to keep connections and BGP sessions healthy, and a calm, repeatable troubleshooting workflow you can run when connectivity fails. We'll study port hours and data transfer out so you can estimate spend, then move into the monitoring signals like ConnectionState and BGPState that surface failures before applications break. Finally, we'll walk a terminal-style troubleshooting simulation that shows the router commands and CloudWatch checks you would run to identify a VLAN mismatch or a BGP peer problem. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes — for example, assuming a physical link is sufficient when BGP is down — and give you clear takeaways to reduce mean time to resolution. By the end of this module, you should be able to predict major cost drivers, set meaningful alarms, and run a structured troubleshooting checklist when a VPC loses reachability to on-premises services.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Direct Connect Overview

Direct Connect — Pricing, Monitoring, and Troubleshooting

Learn the cost drivers, CloudWatch metrics, and a step-by-step troubleshooting workflow to keep hybrid connectivity resilient and cost-effective.

In this lesson
Estimate costs, monitor metrics, and run diagnostics.
Coming up
CloudWatch dashboards, alarms, and CLI checks.
Quick Orientation

This chapter emphasizes a calm, layered troubleshooting flow: verify physical link, confirm VLAN and Layer 2, then inspect BGP and route propagation. Cost decisions balance port hours against data transfer out volume.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
16:9 HD Classroom
Pricing
Port hours and data transfer out are primary cost drivers.
Monitoring
CloudWatch metrics like BGPState and ConnectionState reveal issues fast.
Troubleshooting
Work from Layer 1 to Layer 3 and validate VLANs, MTU, and BGP peers.
Use the upcoming screens to practice CLI checks and build a dashboard.

For each objective I’ll include why it matters: cost knowledge avoids surprises and monitoring helps you detect service degradation early. These outcomes map directly to operational tasks you’ll perform when a production hybrid path fails.

screens.title: Direct Connect Pricing — Port Hours and DTO
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s define the two primary cost drivers for Direct Connect and why each matters in budgeting and architecture. Port hours are a fixed hourly charge tied to the physical or logical Direct Connect port you provision. Regardless of traffic, that port hour accrues cost whenever the connection exists — so idle circuits still cost money. Dedicated connections usually carry higher port-hour rates than hosted connections because you pay for exclusive capacity. Data Transfer Out, or DTO, is the variable charge for data leaving AWS over Direct Connect. DTO is typically lower than internet egress rates and is often tiered by volume, producing meaningful savings for sustained large transfers. In practice you should model both: a small, steady DTO with an expensive port, or a high DTO and moderate port cost will produce different break-even points. A common misconception is to only watch DTO — without accounting for port hours you can incur significant idle cost. Example: a 1 Gbps port billed hourly plus 20 TB of outbound traffic will have both line-item charges. Takeaway: always run a port-plus-payload estimate and consider scheduled shutdowns or lower-capacity ports for infrequently used links.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Pricing — Port Hours & DTO
Definition

Port Hours: an hourly charge per Direct Connect port. Data Transfer Out: variable egress cost from AWS across Direct Connect, usually tiered and cheaper than public internet egress.

Example Estimate
Model both hourly port cost and DTO for expected monthly TB. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator to combine these figures.
Key Takeaway

Port hours can dominate costs for idle circuits; DTO matters most for consistent heavy egress.

Pricing Breakdown
Port Hours
Fixed hourly rate by speed. Applies while port exists, even if idle.
Data Transfer Out
Variable egress pricing, often tiered by TB. Data in is typically free.
VIF / DX Gateway
VIFs and DX Gateways do not usually have separate hourly port charges; DTO still applies for attached VPCs.
Common Mistake

Overlooking port hours for seldom-used connections is common. If you expect low traffic, consider resizing or scheduling downtime.

screens.title: CloudWatch Metrics for Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring Direct Connect uses CloudWatch metrics that tell you whether the physical link and routing plane are healthy. Begin with ConnectionState: this metric indicates the physical state of the Direct Connect link. A value of zero typically means down; non-zero indicates up. Next is BGPState: this metric shows whether the BGP session for a virtual interface is established. A physical link can be up while BGP is down, and that combination explains many connectivity incidents. Also monitor ConnectionBpsIn and ConnectionBpsOut to track throughput trends and detect saturation, and VirtualInterfaceBpsIn and VirtualInterfaceBpsOut to see which VIF is consuming bandwidth. ConnectionErrorCount and ConnectionLightLevelTx/Rx are important for fiber diagnostics and physical errors. A practical example: create a CloudWatch dashboard with these metrics for each connection and add alarms for ConnectionState and BGPState transitions to receive SNS notifications. Misconception to avoid: assuming bandwidth metrics alone indicate health — they show traffic but not whether routes are exchanged. Final takeaway: instrument both link health and BGP state and test alerts so on-call responders know the next action. CloudWatch Metrics for Direct Connect means track connectionstate and bgpstate plus bandwidth and error metrics so you detect both physical and logical failures.. In practical terms, key metrics to track connection and vif health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › CloudWatch Metrics
Metric Reference
  • ConnectionState: physical link up/down indicator.
  • BGPState: BGP session status for VIFs; up or down.
  • ConnectionBpsIn/Out: throughput for the whole connection.
  • VirtualInterfaceBpsIn/Out: per-VIF bandwidth usage.
  • ConnectionErrorCount and LightLevelTx/Rx: physical layer diagnostics.
Key Takeaway

Alarms should cover both ConnectionState and BGPState so you know whether to escalate the fiber vendor or the BGP configuration team.

Example CLI
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/DirectConnect \
  --metric-name BGPState \
  --dimensions Name=VirtualInterfaceId,Value=dxvif-abcdefghij \
  --start-time 2023-01-01T00:00:00Z \
  --end-time 2023-01-01T01:00:00Z \
  --period 300 \
  --statistic Average \
  --region us-east-1
Interpretation: a returned value of 1 means BGP is up; 0 means BGP is down. Use these calls to populate dashboards or runbooks during incident response.

screens.title: CloudWatch Alarms and Dashboards
screens.narratorSegment: Designing dashboards and alarms is about making the right people act at the right time. Start by selecting a minimal set of critical metrics: ConnectionState and BGPState are alarm-worthy because they represent immediate loss of connectivity. Next add bandwidth counters and error counts to diagnose congestion or physical faults. For each alarm, choose a threshold that avoids noisy alerts while still catching real issues — for example, create an alarm for BGPState equal to zero for two consecutive periods, rather than a single transient drop. Route notifications to an SNS topic that lists network owners and on-call engineers, and include a concise playbook in the notification payload or a linked runbook reference. A dashboard should group related metrics per Direct Connect connection and include per-VIF tiles so you can see which virtual interface is affected. Example: a dashboard row with ConnectionState, BGPState, VirtualInterfaceBpsOut, and ConnectionErrorCount gives a quick triage view. Misconception: many teams create bandwidth-only alerts; these miss BGP or VLAN mismatches. Final question to reflect on: when an alarm fires, who has permission and knowledge to run the immediate follow-up checks?

keyIdea.text: Alert on the presence or absence of routes and links, not just traffic levels, and tie notifications to runbooks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Alarms & Dashboards
Alarm Design Steps
  1. Select critical metrics: ConnectionState and BGPState first.
  2. Set thresholds with short confirmation windows to avoid flaps.
  3. Route alerts to SNS with runbook links and escalation contacts.
  4. Create dashboards with per-connection and per-VIF tiles for quick triage.
Key Takeaway

Focus alerts on link and routing failures and verify that notifications include a next-step for responders.

Example Dashboard Row
Tiles: ConnectionState | BGPState | VirtualInterfaceBpsOut | ConnectionErrorCount
This row helps decide: is this a physical fault, a BGP problem, or just traffic load?

screens.title: A Layered Troubleshooting Approach
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting Direct Connect is most reliable when you follow a layered sequence: physical layer, data link layer, then network/BGP layer. At Layer 1, confirm ConnectionState in CloudWatch and verify cross-connects with your colocation provider. Check light levels and cables for fiber issues. At Layer 2, verify VLAN IDs and that the VLAN configured on your on-prem router matches the VIF configuration in AWS — VLAN mismatches are a very common cause of VIF failures. Also confirm MTU and jumbo frame settings on both sides when large frames are expected. At Layer 3, inspect BGP: check peer IP addresses, ASN, authentication keys, and the neighbor state on your router using commands like show ip bgp summary. Also validate route propagation and check for overlapping CIDRs that could prevent proper routing. A typical misconception is to assume that an 'up' physical link guarantees connectivity; without BGP established, traffic won't flow. Concrete example: if ConnectionState is up but BGPState is down, focus on BGP config items such as ASN or peer IP first. The key insight: a methodical top-down approach narrows root cause faster than random checks.

keyIdea.title: Top-down triage
keyIdea.text: Start with physical checks, then Layer 2 VLAN and MTU, then confirm BGP and routes to resolve outages reliably.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Layered Troubleshooting
Layer Checklist
  • Layer 1: Check ConnectionState, light levels, LOA-CFA, fiber cables.
  • Layer 2: Verify VLAN IDs, MAC learning, and MTU / jumbo frames.
  • Layer 3: Confirm BGPState, peer IPs, ASN, auth key, and route tables.
Concrete Scenario
If ConnectionState shows up but BGPState is down, run a BGP neighbor check on your router and verify the /30 peering IPs and ASN. If IPs or ASN mismatch, BGP won't form even when the fiber works.
Common Mistake

Assuming the link is healthy because it is up at the physical layer; always confirm BGP to validate end-to-end routing.

screens.title: Router Commands and BGP Checks
screens.narratorSegment: When BGP is suspected, certain router commands give immediate insight. Use show ip interface brief to verify interface IPs and administrative state. Use show vlan brief to confirm VLAN assignments and match them to the VIF configuration in AWS. Then use show ip bgp summary or show bgp neighbors to check neighbor state, uptime, and the number of received routes. When you run ping to the AWS BGP peer IP, a successful ping validates reachability at Layer 3 but does not guarantee BGP will form if credentials or ASNs are incorrect. Example output to look for: a BGP neighbor state of established and a positive count of received prefixes indicates valid route exchange. If you see idle, active, or connect states, inspect ACLs, authentication keys, and interface reachability. Misconception: seeing learned routes on the router always means VPC traffic will follow the same path; ensure route tables and propagation are configured correctly. A final practical tip: capture and log the exact neighbor outputs to include in any support ticket to AWS or your colo provider. Router Commands and BGP Checks means use targeted router commands to validate interface, vlan, and bgp neighbor states and collect outputs for escalation.. In practical terms, practical commands and how to interpret their output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Router Diagnostics
Essential Commands
  • show ip interface brief — verify interface IPs and up/down state.
  • show vlan brief — confirm VLAN assignment matches VIF.
  • show ip bgp summary — BGP peer state, uptime, prefix counts.
  • ping & traceroute — test reachability to BGP peer and beyond.
Example Router Output
# show ip bgp summary
Neighbor        V    AS MsgRcvd MsgSent  TblVer  InQ OutQ Up/Down  State/PfxRcd
10.0.0.2        4 65002   1234   1210       0    0    0 02:14:55        120
Interpretation: 'State/PfxRcd' shows prefixes received. A non-zero value with an Up time indicates a working adjacency and advertised routes.

screens.title: VLAN ID and MTU Mismatches
screens.narratorSegment: Layer 2 mismatches are frequent and often quick to fix once identified. A VLAN ID mismatch occurs when the VLAN configured on the customer router does not match the VLAN assigned to the Virtual Interface in AWS. This prevents frames from reaching the correct VIF and often manifests as a VIF that never moves to an operational state. To diagnose, verify the VLAN ID on your router, check the VIF configuration in AWS, and confirm with show vlan brief output. MTU mismatches are another trap, especially when jumbo frames are enabled. If one side expects an MTU of 9001 and the other is set to 1500, larger packets can be dropped or cause PMTU issues that break application flows. Practical example: after a maintenance window, you observe that VIFs are not passing traffic — if ConnectionState is up but no traffic flows and pings to the peer fail, suspect VLAN mismatch first. Misconception: swapping cables or reloading equipment without checking VLANs can mask the real issue. Takeaway: verify Layer 2 settings early in your checklist and document VLAN assignments in your runbook.

keyIdea.title: Match layer 2 settings
keyIdea.text: Verify VLAN IDs and MTU on both sides; mismatches prevent the VIF from carrying traffic even when the physical link is up.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › VLAN & MTU Issues
VLAN Mismatch

Ensure the VLAN ID on your on-prem router matches the VIF VLAN in AWS. Mismatches prevent frames from reaching the intended virtual interface.

Check: show vlan brief | Compare to VIF config
MTU & Jumbo Frames

If jumbo frames are enabled, ensure both sides support the same MTU. Mismatches cause fragmentation or dropped packets and can appear as performance problems.

Check: interface MTU values and application packet sizes
Real-world scenario
After maintenance, ConnectionState is up but pings to the peer timeout. Evidence points to a VLAN ID mismatch — verify VLANs before escalating to the colo provider.

screens.title: Physical vs Logical Failures
screens.narratorSegment: Distinguishing physical failures from logical or configuration faults saves time during an incident. Physical failures — fiber cuts, misconnected cross-connects, or transceiver faults — usually present as ConnectionState down and may show increased ConnectionErrorCount or abnormal light level readings. Logical failures — VLAN mismatches, ACLs, or BGP misconfiguration — can show a ConnectionState up while BGPState is down or no prefixes are received. A simple diagnosis flow: first check ConnectionState and physical indicators; if the link is down, coordinate with the colocation provider and inspect light levels and cabling. If the link is up, pivot to Layer 2 and 3 checks: confirm VLANs, MTU, then BGP peer IPs, ASN, and authentication keys. Example: customers often see an 'up' physical link after new cabling but no traffic; this frequently turns out to be a VLAN ID mismatch or a misconfigured subinterface. Misconception: believing that faster optics or clean transceivers always fix logical issues. Key insight: read the metrics to know which team to engage first — colo/vendor for physical faults, network engineering for BGP and VLAN issues. Physical vs Logical Failures means connectionstate and physical diagnostics indicate vendor escalation; bgpstate and config checks point to network engineering.. narration.text: Distinguishing physical failures from logical or configuration faults saves time during an incident. Physical failures — fiber cuts, misconnected cross-connects, or transceiver faults — usually present as ConnectionState down and may show increased ConnectionErrorCount or abnormal light level readings. screens.title: Terminal Demo — Finding a VLAN Mismatch
screens.narratorSegment: In this terminal-style walkthrough, we’ll simulate a practical troubleshooting sequence that reveals a VLAN mismatch. Start with CloudWatch: ConnectionState reports up, BGPState is down. That tells us the link is live but routing isn’t established. On the router, run show ip interface brief to confirm the interface is administratively up and has the expected IP. Next use show vlan brief to see which VLANs are active and whether the interface is assigned to the expected VLAN. If the router shows the interface on VLAN 100 but the AWS VIF is configured for VLAN 101, the mismatch is the root cause. You would then coordinate with your change control or the colo team to correct the VLAN. screens.title: Sizing and Cost Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a Direct Connect solution you must balance performance needs against ongoing costs. Port speed determines both throughput and port hour cost — higher speeds cost more per hour but can reduce DTO if large transfers complete faster, which sometimes lowers overall expense. Decide between dedicated and hosted connections based on control and budget: dedicated provides exclusive capacity and usually higher port-hour rates; hosted can be cheaper but shares provider infrastructure. Also model expected DTO patterns: sustained high egress favors Direct Connect due to reduced DTO rates, while sporadic transfers may not justify a high-cost port. Consider failover and redundancy strategies: dual ports in separate locations increase port-hour costs but significantly improve availability and reduce risk of single-point failure. Practical example: if you move a nightly 50 TB backup to Direct Connect, compute monthly DTO at tiered rates and compare against internet egress costs and the additional port-hour charges for redundancy. Misconception: selecting maximum speed for headroom without modeling DTO often increases cost without proportional benefit. Takeaway: size ports to expected steady-state workloads and include redundancy when availability requirements demand it.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build practical fluency with the operational side of AWS Direct Connect. You will learn the pricing components that drive cost decisions, how to use CloudWatch metrics to keep connections and BGP sessions healthy, and a calm, repeatable troubleshooting workflow you can run when connectivity fails. We'll study port hours and data transfer out so you can estimate spend, then move into the monitoring signals like ConnectionState and BGPState that surface failures before applications break. Finally, we'll walk a terminal-style troubleshooting simulation that shows the router commands and CloudWatch checks you would run to identify a VLAN mismatch or a BGP peer problem. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes — for example, assuming a physical link is sufficient when BGP is down — and give you clear takeaways to reduce mean time to resolution. By the end of this module, you should be able to predict major cost drivers, set meaningful alarms, and run a structured troubleshooting checklist when a VPC loses reachability to on-premises services.

In this first objectives screen I’ll set clear, measurable outcomes you can use to show competency. First, you will be able to identify the key Direct Connect cost components and explain which ones drive recurring spend. That means naming port hours and data transfer out, and giving an example estimate for a given bandwidth and monthly transfer. Second, you will know how to read and interpret CloudWatch metrics for Direct Connect and VIFs, including what ConnectionState and BGPState values mean in practice. For each objective I’ll include why it matters: cost knowledge avoids surprises and monitoring helps you detect service degradation early. These objectives also include a verification step: you should be able to create a CloudWatch alarm for BGPState going down and explain the notification flow through SNS. Finally, you will be able to describe a structured troubleshooting flow for Direct Connect outages, from physical diagnostics to BGP neighbor checks. These outcomes map directly to operational tasks you’ll perform when a production hybrid path fails.

This second objectives screen gives practical verification steps and mnemonic aids you can use during incidents. For cost awareness, practice using the AWS Pricing Calculator and check both port hours and monthly data transfer estimates; think of the mnemonic 'Port plus Payload' to remember the fixed and variable components. For monitoring, set alarms on ConnectionState and BGPState and label them clearly so on-call staff know whether to escalate the network team or the datacenter contact. For troubleshooting, use the layered mnemonic 'C, V, B' — Connection, VLAN, BGP — as your first three checks. For routing validation, practice verifying BGP peer IPs, ASN, and route propagation across VPC route tables and your router tables. Each card here includes a small visual hint so you can recall the steps during a high-pressure outage. These verification milestones help you convert knowledge into measurable actions you can sign off during a post-incident review.

Let’s define the two primary cost drivers for Direct Connect and why each matters in budgeting and architecture. Port hours are a fixed hourly charge tied to the physical or logical Direct Connect port you provision. Regardless of traffic, that port hour accrues cost whenever the connection exists — so idle circuits still cost money. Dedicated connections usually carry higher port-hour rates than hosted connections because you pay for exclusive capacity. Data Transfer Out, or DTO, is the variable charge for data leaving AWS over Direct Connect. DTO is typically lower than internet egress rates and is often tiered by volume, producing meaningful savings for sustained large transfers. In practice you should model both: a small, steady DTO with an expensive port, or a high DTO and moderate port cost will produce different break-even points. A common misconception is to only watch DTO — without accounting for port hours you can incur significant idle cost. Example: a 1 Gbps port billed hourly plus 20 TB of outbound traffic will have both line-item charges. Takeaway: always run a port-plus-payload estimate and consider scheduled shutdowns or lower-capacity ports for infrequently used links.

Monitoring Direct Connect uses CloudWatch metrics that tell you whether the physical link and routing plane are healthy. Begin with ConnectionState: this metric indicates the physical state of the Direct Connect link. A value of zero typically means down; non-zero indicates up. Next is BGPState: this metric shows whether the BGP session for a virtual interface is established. A physical link can be up while BGP is down, and that combination explains many connectivity incidents. Also monitor ConnectionBpsIn and ConnectionBpsOut to track throughput trends and detect saturation, and VirtualInterfaceBpsIn and VirtualInterfaceBpsOut to see which VIF is consuming bandwidth. ConnectionErrorCount and ConnectionLightLevelTx/Rx are important for fiber diagnostics and physical errors. A practical example: create a CloudWatch dashboard with these metrics for each connection and add alarms for ConnectionState and BGPState transitions to receive SNS notifications. Misconception to avoid: assuming bandwidth metrics alone indicate health — they show traffic but not whether routes are exchanged. Final takeaway: instrument both link health and BGP state and test alerts so on-call responders know the next action. Designing dashboards and alarms is about making the right people act at the right time. Start by selecting a minimal set of critical metrics: ConnectionState and BGPState are alarm-worthy because they represent immediate loss of connectivity. Next add bandwidth counters and error counts to diagnose congestion or physical faults. For each alarm, choose a threshold that avoids noisy alerts while still catching real issues — for example, create an alarm for BGPState equal to zero for two consecutive periods, rather than a single transient drop. Route notifications to an SNS topic that lists network owners and on-call engineers, and include a concise playbook in the notification payload or a linked runbook reference. A dashboard should group related metrics per Direct Connect connection and include per-VIF tiles so you can see which virtual interface is affected. Example: a dashboard row with ConnectionState, BGPState, VirtualInterfaceBpsOut, and ConnectionErrorCount gives a quick triage view. Misconception: many teams create bandwidth-only alerts; these miss BGP or VLAN mismatches. Final question to reflect on: when an alarm fires, who has permission and knowledge to run the immediate follow-up checks?

Troubleshooting Direct Connect is most reliable when you follow a layered sequence: physical layer, data link layer, then network/BGP layer. At Layer 1, confirm ConnectionState in CloudWatch and verify cross-connects with your colocation provider. Check light levels and cables for fiber issues. At Layer 2, verify VLAN IDs and that the VLAN configured on your on-prem router matches the VIF configuration in AWS — VLAN mismatches are a very common cause of VIF failures. Also confirm MTU and jumbo frame settings on both sides when large frames are expected. At Layer 3, inspect BGP: check peer IP addresses, ASN, authentication keys, and the neighbor state on your router using commands like show ip bgp summary. Also validate route propagation and check for overlapping CIDRs that could prevent proper routing. A typical misconception is to assume that an 'up' physical link guarantees connectivity; without BGP established, traffic won't flow. Concrete example: if ConnectionState is up but BGPState is down, focus on BGP config items such as ASN or peer IP first. The key insight: a methodical top-down approach narrows root cause faster than random checks.

When BGP is suspected, certain router commands give immediate insight. Use show ip interface brief to verify interface IPs and administrative state. Use show vlan brief to confirm VLAN assignments and match them to the VIF configuration in AWS. Then use show ip bgp summary or show bgp neighbors to check neighbor state, uptime, and the number of received routes. When you run ping to the AWS BGP peer IP, a successful ping validates reachability at Layer 3 but does not guarantee BGP will form if credentials or ASNs are incorrect. Example output to look for: a BGP neighbor state of established and a positive count of received prefixes indicates valid route exchange. If you see idle, active, or connect states, inspect ACLs, authentication keys, and interface reachability. Misconception: seeing learned routes on the router always means VPC traffic will follow the same path; ensure route tables and propagation are configured correctly. When designing a Direct Connect solution you must balance performance needs against ongoing costs. Port speed determines both throughput and port hour cost — higher speeds cost more per hour but can reduce DTO if large transfers complete faster, which sometimes lowers overall expense. Decide between dedicated and hosted connections based on control and budget: dedicated provides exclusive capacity and usually higher port-hour rates; hosted can be cheaper but shares provider infrastructure. Also model expected DTO patterns: sustained high egress favors Direct Connect due to reduced DTO rates, while sporadic transfers may not justify a high-cost port. Consider failover and redundancy strategies: dual ports in separate locations increase port-hour costs but significantly improve availability and reduce risk of single-point failure. Practical example: if you move a nightly 50 TB backup to Direct Connect, compute monthly DTO at tiered rates and compare against internet egress costs and the additional port-hour charges for redundancy. Misconception: selecting maximum speed for headroom without modeling DTO often increases cost without proportional benefit. Takeaway: size ports to expected steady-state workloads and include redundancy when availability requirements demand it.

Let’s summarize the most important ideas to carry forward. First, Direct Connect costs are driven primarily by port hours — a fixed hourly charge — and Data Transfer Out — a variable, often tiered egress rate. Second, CloudWatch is your primary telemetry source; monitor ConnectionState and BGPState alongside bandwidth and error metrics to detect both physical and logical issues. Third, troubleshooting should follow a layered flow: verify the physical link, confirm Layer 2 VLAN and MTU, then inspect BGP session health and route propagation. Fourth, common failure modes include VLAN mismatches, incorrect BGP peering IPs or ASN, and forgotten port-hour costs for idle circuits. Use dashboards, alarms, and runbooks to reduce mean time to resolution. Keep your incident responses evidence-based: capture CloudWatch snapshots and router outputs before making changes, and include them when escalating to vendors or AWS Support. These practices reduce cost surprises and make hybrid connectivity dependable.
